basis: Words that reach the reservation: section 10(a) of the Philippine Independence Act directs the surrender of 'all right of possession, supervision, jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty' over the Islands, 'including all military and other reservations of the Government of the United States in the Philippines (except such naval reservations and fueling stations as are reserved under section 5)'; Proclamation 2695 of July 4, 1946, 'subject to the reservations provided for in the applicable statutes', states that the United States 'hereby withdraws and surrenders all rights of possession, supervision, jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty now existing and exercised' over the territory; and Article I of the Treaty of General Relations (in force October 22, 1946) withdraws and surrenders all such rights 'except the use of such bases, necessary appurtenances to such bases, and the right incident thereto, as the United States of America, by agreement with the Republic of the Philippines, may deem necessary to retain'. The agreement so made, the Military Bases Agreement in force March 26, 1947, retains the use of the bases listed in Annex A (and Annex B on necessity), which do not include this member's place; keeps the Port of Manila reservation (art. XXI(2)); and keeps only one other class outside the bases: 'temporary quarters and installations now existing outside the bases ... for such reasonable time, not exceeding two years', with any extension fixed by agreement, barred for the City of Manila, and one that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years' (art. XXI(1)). Member test: the reservation lies in the Philippine Islands, is an Army reservation, and its place is neither an Annex A or B base nor the Port of Manila reservation. Whether U.S. forces still occupied an installation on this member's land in 1947 is not known from the fields held; if they did, art. XXI(1) let them stay at most two years plus an extension of at most three years, so the U.S. right over the land ended no later than five years after the agreement took effect.

date.basis: No later than the outer limit of art. XXI(1) of the 1947 Military Bases Agreement: two years plus an extension that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years', counted from the agreement's entry into force on 1947-03-26 (on the narrower reading that three years is the whole period, 1950-03-26; for temporary installations within the City of Manila, where no extension was allowed, 1949-03-26). July 4, 1946 (Proclamation 2695) or October 22, 1946 (Treaty art. I) for a member whose land held no U.S. installation in 1947; earlier if a later order revoked or restored the lands.

gaps: The Treaty of General Relations (61 Stat. 1174) and the Military Bases Agreement (61 Stat. 4019; 43 U.N.T.S. No. 673) are read on the web only; acquire them.

Note V of the 1947 agreement, in full: 'I have the honor to state, in signing the Agreement of March 14, 1947, Between the United States of America and the Republic of the Philippines Concerning Military Bases, the understanding of my Government that the question of the adjustment of any rights and titles held by the United States pursuant to the provisions of the Act of Congress of March 24, 1934 (48 Stat. 456) as amended, specifically Section 10(b) thereof, the Joint Resolution of the Congress of June 29, 1944, and the Act of Congress of July 3, 1946, and Treaties and Agreements heretofore entered into between the United States and the Philippines, to real property in any of the bases covered by the aforementioned Agreement or any naval reservations or fueling stations not so covered is reserved and will be settled subsequently in accordance with the terms of the Acts and Joint Resolution of the Congress mentioned above.' (61 Stat. 4033; Note VI, the Philippine reply, concurs 'without conceding the existence of any rights or titles to the real property therein referred to'.) Note V reserves title questions for the bases and for naval reservations outside them (the latter routed to B20n); it does not reserve the possession and control of an Army reservation outside the bases, which Article I surrendered. Section 5 of the 1934 Act likewise kept designated reservation lands out of the 1935 grant to the Commonwealth. Any U.S. title that outlasted the surrender is a property question disclosed here, not a continuation of the reservation.

The joint resolution of June 29, 1944 (58 Stat. 626) is read on the web only; which bases, if any, the President withheld under it before July 4, 1946 is not established in the sources held. A withheld base is retained only through the 1947 agreement, so the interval's bound covers it.

Which members' lands held U.S. temporary installations in March 1947 is not known; the interval's upper bound assumes the widest reading of art. XXI(1). A later agreement extending a temporary installation beyond the art. XXI(1) limit would be a new instrument; none is held.

For Manila members: Proclamation 2694 of July 3, 1946 (closing part on the held 60 Stat. 1352 page; number, title and authority read on the Truman Library copy; opening page not verified) designated nine Manila properties for U.S. diplomatic and consular establishments under section 10 of the 1934 Act as amended in 1939; any U.S. use of such a property rests on that proclamation, not on a military reservation order.

EO 1437 (Regan Barracks target range) was placed under the Government of the Philippine Islands by EO 3086 of 1919, 'subject to such reimbursement and reservations as may be prescribed by the Secretary of War'; because of that proviso the class interval is kept. EO 1628 (Fort Pikit and Fort Reina Regente) appears to have been transferred by EO 3056 of 1919-03-03 (see branch C28).

EO 985 carries a held 'amendment' edge from EO 10069 (1949), which amends 'Executive Order No. 985 of November 25, 1946' on travel expenses; that is a different order (a misprint of the number), so the edge does not act on EO 985. The engine flags it (acted_on_after_lead_end).

basis: Words that reach the reservation: section 10(a) of the Philippine Independence Act directs the surrender of 'all right of possession, supervision, jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty' over the Islands, 'including all military and other reservations of the Government of the United States in the Philippines (except such naval reservations and fueling stations as are reserved under section 5)'; Proclamation 2695 of July 4, 1946, 'subject to the reservations provided for in the applicable statutes', states that the United States 'hereby withdraws and surrenders all rights of possession, supervision, jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty now existing and exercised' over the territory; and Article I of the Treaty of General Relations (in force October 22, 1946) withdraws and surrenders all such rights 'except the use of such bases, necessary appurtenances to such bases, and the right incident thereto, as the United States of America, by agreement with the Republic of the Philippines, may deem necessary to retain'. The agreement so made, the Military Bases Agreement in force March 26, 1947, retains the use of the bases listed in Annex A (and Annex B on necessity), which do not include this member's place; keeps the Port of Manila reservation (art. XXI(2)); and keeps only one other class outside the bases: 'temporary quarters and installations now existing outside the bases ... for such reasonable time, not exceeding two years', with any extension fixed by agreement, barred for the City of Manila, and one that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years' (art. XXI(1)). Member test: the reservation lies in the Philippine Islands, is an Army reservation, and its place is neither an Annex A or B base nor the Port of Manila reservation. Whether U.S. forces still occupied an installation on this member's land in 1947 is not known from the fields held; if they did, art. XXI(1) let them stay at most two years plus an extension of at most three years, so the U.S. right over the land ended no later than five years after the agreement took effect.

date.basis: No later than the outer limit of art. XXI(1) of the 1947 Military Bases Agreement: two years plus an extension that 'shall in no case exceed a period of three years', counted from the agreement's entry into force on 1947-03-26 (on the narrower reading that three years is the whole period, 1950-03-26; for temporary installations within the City of Manila, where no extension was allowed, 1949-03-26). July 4, 1946 (Proclamation 2695) or October 22, 1946 (Treaty art. I) for a member whose land held no U.S. installation in 1947; earlier if a later order revoked or restored the lands.

gaps: The Treaty of General Relations (61 Stat. 1174) and the Military Bases Agreement (61 Stat. 4019; 43 U.N.T.S. No. 673) are read on the web only; acquire them.

Note V of the 1947 agreement, in full: 'I have the honor to state, in signing the Agreement of March 14, 1947, Between the United States of America and the Republic of the Philippines Concerning Military Bases, the understanding of my Government that the question of the adjustment of any rights and titles held by the United States pursuant to the provisions of the Act of Congress of March 24, 1934 (48 Stat. 456) as amended, specifically Section 10(b) thereof, the Joint Resolution of the Congress of June 29, 1944, and the Act of Congress of July 3, 1946, and Treaties and Agreements heretofore entered into between the United States and the Philippines, to real property in any of the bases covered by the aforementioned Agreement or any naval reservations or fueling stations not so covered is reserved and will be settled subsequently in accordance with the terms of the Acts and Joint Resolution of the Congress mentioned above.' (61 Stat. 4033; Note VI, the Philippine reply, concurs 'without conceding the existence of any rights or titles to the real property therein referred to'.) Note V reserves title questions for the bases and for naval reservations outside them (the latter routed to B20n); it does not reserve the possession and control of an Army reservation outside the bases, which Article I surrendered. Section 5 of the 1934 Act likewise kept designated reservation lands out of the 1935 grant to the Commonwealth. Any U.S. title that outlasted the surrender is a property question disclosed here, not a continuation of the reservation.

The joint resolution of June 29, 1944 (58 Stat. 626) is read on the web only; which bases, if any, the President withheld under it before July 4, 1946 is not established in the sources held. A withheld base is retained only through the 1947 agreement, so the interval's bound covers it.

Which members' lands held U.S. temporary installations in March 1947 is not known; the interval's upper bound assumes the widest reading of art. XXI(1). A later agreement extending a temporary installation beyond the art. XXI(1) limit would be a new instrument; none is held.

For Manila members: Proclamation 2694 of July 3, 1946 (closing part on the held 60 Stat. 1352 page; number, title and authority read on the Truman Library copy; opening page not verified) designated nine Manila properties for U.S. diplomatic and consular establishments under section 10 of the 1934 Act as amended in 1939; any U.S. use of such a property rests on that proclamation, not on a military reservation order.

EO 1437 (Regan Barracks target range) was placed under the Government of the Philippine Islands by EO 3086 of 1919, 'subject to such reimbursement and reservations as may be prescribed by the Secretary of War'; because of that proviso the class interval is kept. EO 1628 (Fort Pikit and Fort Reina Regente) appears to have been transferred by EO 3056 of 1919-03-03 (see branch C28).

EO 985 carries a held 'amendment' edge from EO 10069 (1949), which amends 'Executive Order No. 985 of November 25, 1946' on travel expenses; that is a different order (a misprint of the number), so the edge does not act on EO 985. The engine flags it (acted_on_after_lead_end).

basis: The order extends the trust period on the lands it covers for a stated number of years, and the whole extended period ran out before 1934-06-18; by its own terms its operation ended then. IRA sec. 2 reaches only trust periods existing on 1934-06-18, so it did not reach this period; any later continuation of the trust on the same land came from a separate later executive order with its own lifecycle, or from a statute named in the gaps.

date.basis: stated expiry plus stated period (see doctrine appendix)

gaps: Later held extension orders naming the same tribe, band or class (each a separate executive order with its own lifecycle; it may cover other allotments): 3250: EO 4694, EO 5305; 3304: EO 3980, EO 5416; 3312: EO 4688, EO 4858, EO 5299, EO 5356, EO 5556.
Expiry year and period are read from the order text (the WPA 1944 summary where the scan is illegible); individual allotment expiry dates are not held, so the end is an interval.

The 25 CFR chapter I appendix (read on the web) lists Acts of Congress continuing trust periods only for Capitan Grande, Pala, Crow, Mexican Kickapoo, Kaw, Quapaw, Klamath River and Yakima lands; none reaches this order's period except as stated in the basis. The Act of June 15, 1935, sec. 3 reaches trust periods on excluded reservations not yet extended past 1936-12-31; a period that had already ended before 1934 was no longer this order's period, so its words do not reach it. IRA sec. 2 reaches only periods existing on 1934-06-18.
EO 3304 (Klamath River, trusts expiring during 1920): the Act of December 24, 1942 reimposes only the period "which expired July 31, 1919" (EO 2943's), not this order's.

basis: The order authorizes (or directs) one disposition of named property under sec. 12 of the Trading with the Enemy Act and sets no deadline. It is spent when the sale, rejection, resale or release is made, and no held record shows that it was made (the one order a held text shows performed, EO 3259, is decided by B03E). The Trading with the Enemy Act is excepted from the 1921 resolution and is still law, and the later transfers of the Custodian's functions (EO 6694 of 1934; EO 9095 and EO 9142 of 1942; EO 9788 of 1946; the 1966 abolition of the Office of Alien Property) moved the functions without extinguishing authorizations, so no class event ends an unexercised authorization.
gaps: The Custodian's report for 1918 to Feb. 15, 1919 and the annual reports for 1919-1934 (S17) would show the sale or rejection for each trust; until one is held the order stays open.
Property returned under the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 254; not held) would make an unexercised authorization moot; that would need its own evidence.
Orders covering several lots or properties need one end per lot.
EO 2832 is a general rule (private sale of merchandise in lots worth no more than $10,000), not a single authorization; it ends only by revocation or supersession, which is not held.

EO 4224-A's only operative clause is 'The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to execute and deliver a quit-claim deed conveying certain interests in real estate' in Cook County, Illinois; amending EO 4073-A appears only among its stated reasons. It is its own single authorization, open here like EO 3923 and EO 4045.

EO 3183 (reject all bids at the Sept. 17, 1919 auction of the same 4,505 First Reinsurance shares): EO 3259 recites that the shares were 'thrice offered at public auction and no satisfactory bid has been received', and EO 3265 records their private sale to another buyer by Apr. 29, 1920. That shows the subject was disposed of by then, but no held text records that the Richter & Company bid was rejected; open pending a coordinator decision whether disposal of the subject ends an unexercised rejection authorization.

EO 3227 (Feb. 13, 1920) authorizes the Custodian to confirm 'in the case of sales heretofore made by him' under the Polk orders of Feb. 26, 1919 (EO 3016C) and Apr. 5, 1919 (EO 3016K). The words are conditional and name no property, so they do not show any particular sale made; EO 3016C, 3016K and 3227 stay open.

EO 3923 carries a held revocation edge from PLO 369 (May 15, 1947, 12 FR 2038; BLM table, PLO text not held): 'revoking EO Nos. 2247, 2658, and 3923; withdrawing lands for Agriculture experimental station'. EO 2247 and 2658 are Alaska agricultural-experiment-station orders; the held EO 3923 is a Custodian sale of Stoehr & Sons shares with no land to revoke. This is a number collision, so the edge does not decide this member; the PLO's '3923' should be traced in the census.
EO 4001 carries a held amendment edge from EO 4045 (1924-07-03); EO 4045 changes the parent's terms, not its performance, and both stay open.

basis: The President set these reservations apart within the Canal Zone, or on adjacent lands whose use the 1903 Isthmian Canal Convention granted. The Panama Canal Treaty of 1977 entered into force on October 1, 1979, terminated and superseded the 1903 Convention (art. I(1)(a)), and returned plenary jurisdiction over the former Zone to Panama (art. XI); but U.S. military forces kept using defense sites under the Agreement in Implementation of Article IV, a new instrument that excepts that property from the transfer (coordinator ruling P5). The Treaty, and with it every U.S. right to use areas in the former Zone, terminated at noon, Panama time, December 31, 1999 (art. II: 'This Treaty shall terminate at noon, Panama time, December 31, 1999'). basis: By its own terms the order performs one act: it takes the named lands out of a military or naval reservation (restoring them, relinquishing them to a territorial or Philippine government, or placing them under the Interior Department for disposal under the Act of July 5, 1884). The act was complete when the order issued; later disposal of the lands proceeds under the statute and the land laws, not under a continuing command of the order (coordinator ruling P1).
gaps: A later order could vacate a transfer to the Interior Department before disposal (EO 1011, EO 2377, EO 2563 and EO 636 did so for EO 803, EO 1422, EO 1279 and EO 372-B); a vacated transfer is ended by the vacating order (branches C09, C16, C23, C24), and the doctrine detects vacatur only where the vacating order is a member of this family. EO 3574 (Fort Davis) is decided by PLO 1712 on its own branch (P22).
Regex screens on the text decide that no reversion, retained right, redefinition or re-reservation is present; scan-OCR texts may hide such a clause.

BLM treated some Alaska transfers under the 1884 Act as continuing withdrawals: PLO 1712 (1958-08-07, held BLM table) revokes EO 3574 'entirely' and EO 7049 (four post cemeteries placed under Interior in 1935, on this branch) 'in part'. Under ruling P1 the transfer is spent on issue and the lead stands; if the owner reads such transfers as withdrawals pending disposal, Alaska members on this branch need the instrument that ended the withdrawal, and EO 7049's other tracts would be open.

Held later edges that act on the land after the order's date do not revive the spent act: EO 477 (1906) redefined the Fort Bayard reservation 'as modified by' EO 341-A; EO 5132 (1929) restored another parcel of the Hawaii Arsenal reservation that EO 3080 had also reduced; EO 4131 (1925) recites the Nulato right-of-way 'turned over to the Department of the Interior' by EO 3418. Each is flagged by the engine (acted_on_after_lead_end) and leaves the lead unchanged.

basis: The order authorizes (or directs) one disposition of named property under sec. 12 of the Trading with the Enemy Act and sets no deadline. It is spent when the sale, rejection, resale or release is made, and no held record shows that it was made (the one order a held text shows performed, EO 3259, is decided by B03E). The Trading with the Enemy Act is excepted from the 1921 resolution and is still law, and the later transfers of the Custodian's functions (EO 6694 of 1934; EO 9095 and EO 9142 of 1942; EO 9788 of 1946; the 1966 abolition of the Office of Alien Property) moved the functions without extinguishing authorizations, so no class event ends an unexercised authorization.
gaps: The Custodian's report for 1918 to Feb. 15, 1919 and the annual reports for 1919-1934 (S17) would show the sale or rejection for each trust; until one is held the order stays open.
Property returned under the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 254; not held) would make an unexercised authorization moot; that would need its own evidence.
Orders covering several lots or properties need one end per lot.
EO 2832 is a general rule (private sale of merchandise in lots worth no more than $10,000), not a single authorization; it ends only by revocation or supersession, which is not held.

EO 4224-A's only operative clause is 'The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to execute and deliver a quit-claim deed conveying certain interests in real estate' in Cook County, Illinois; amending EO 4073-A appears only among its stated reasons. It is its own single authorization, open here like EO 3923 and EO 4045.

EO 3183 (reject all bids at the Sept. 17, 1919 auction of the same 4,505 First Reinsurance shares): EO 3259 recites that the shares were 'thrice offered at public auction and no satisfactory bid has been received', and EO 3265 records their private sale to another buyer by Apr. 29, 1920. That shows the subject was disposed of by then, but no held text records that the Richter & Company bid was rejected; open pending a coordinator decision whether disposal of the subject ends an unexercised rejection authorization.

EO 3227 (Feb. 13, 1920) authorizes the Custodian to confirm 'in the case of sales heretofore made by him' under the Polk orders of Feb. 26, 1919 (EO 3016C) and Apr. 5, 1919 (EO 3016K). The words are conditional and name no property, so they do not show any particular sale made; EO 3016C, 3016K and 3227 stay open.

EO 3923 carries a held revocation edge from PLO 369 (May 15, 1947, 12 FR 2038; BLM table, PLO text not held): 'revoking EO Nos. 2247, 2658, and 3923; withdrawing lands for Agriculture experimental station'. EO 2247 and 2658 are Alaska agricultural-experiment-station orders; the held EO 3923 is a Custodian sale of Stoehr & Sons shares with no land to revoke. This is a number collision, so the edge does not decide this member; the PLO's '3923' should be traced in the census.
EO 4001 carries a held amendment edge from EO 4045 (1924-07-03); EO 4045 changes the parent's terms, not its performance, and both stay open.

EO 2729-A is a multi-part order. Its Censorship Board part was ended by EO 3132 (B03). Its War Trade Board part has a disclosed candidate end: the National Archives records the Board as abolished effective June 30, 1919 under EO 3059 and 3086-A (S11, not held). Its other parts remain open.

EO 2729-A's held revocation edges are partial by their own words: EO 2801 revokes its paragraph XXX and substitutes a new one; EO 2837 revokes the Secretary of the Treasury's licensing power under its section XI (and EO 3180 later rescinds EO 2837); EO 3016 vests in Frank L. Polk the President's sec. 12 powers. None revokes EO 2729-A as a whole, so none decides it.
EO 2744 carries a held amendment edge from EO 3016 (1918-12-03); a partial change does not decide it.

EO 3016 carries held 'amendment' edges from EO 3016F, 3016P, 3016Q, 3016S, 3016T and 3016X: these are Frank L. Polk's sale and rejection orders, which recite EO 3016 as the source of his authority; they exercise the delegation rather than amend it. EO 2729-A also carries an amendment edge from EO 4862 (1928-04-23, supplemental); EO 2770 and 2796 carry cross-reference edges only. None ends a member.

basis: A refuge reservation continues until revoked; renaming (1940) and transfer to Interior (1939) continue it; if the area was in the Refuge System on or after January 1, 1975, 16 U.S.C. 668dd(a)(6) keeps it until Congress acts (subject to the statute's exceptions for acquired-land disposals, exchanges and cooperative agreements), and 43 U.S.C. 1714(j) bars the Secretary from revoking a withdrawal that added lands to the System before October 21, 1976. Whether the order's lands were still reserved in 1975 is not shown by the fields held.
gaps: Needed: evidence that the order's area was in the Refuge System on or after 1975-01-01 (FWS Annual Report of Lands for 1975 and the current year, matched to the order by a reviewed crosswalk) or a PLO revoking it.

Several such orders were revoked in part by PLOs (EO 2446 by PLO 2291, EO 4519 by PLO 988, EO 7106 by PLO 4641 and amended by PLO 1511, EO 7489 by PLO 3385); a partial revocation leaves the order in force as amended.

only-content test: the WPA summary shows nothing but an amendment (no waiver, special rule, promulgation, prescription, construction or extension); the member's operative text uses amending words in an operative form ('is hereby amended', 'strike out', 'by adding', 'to read as follows'; title words such as 'Amending' do not count); and the text has none of the markers of a further provision (present or continued incumbents or occupants, persons now holding, serving or employed, 'it is further ordered', 'the effect of this amendment', status given to persons, a saving for incumbents). A pattern scan of all B12-B15 texts with this marker list was the measure of the test; an unmarked further provision in other words would still escape it

basis: The order extends the trust period on the lands it covers for a stated number of years, and the whole extended period ran out before 1934-06-18; by its own terms its operation ended then. IRA sec. 2 reaches only trust periods existing on 1934-06-18, so it did not reach this period; any later continuation of the trust on the same land came from a separate later executive order with its own lifecycle, or from a statute named in the gaps.

date.basis: stated expiry plus stated period (see doctrine appendix)

gaps: Later held extension orders naming the same tribe, band or class (each a separate executive order with its own lifecycle; it may cover other allotments): 3327: EO 3363, EO 5539; 3301: EO 3447, EO 5415, EO 5626.
Expiry year and period are read from the order text (the WPA 1944 summary where the scan is illegible); individual allotment expiry dates are not held, so the end is an interval.

The 25 CFR chapter I appendix (read on the web) lists Acts of Congress continuing trust periods only for Capitan Grande, Pala, Crow, Mexican Kickapoo, Kaw, Quapaw, Klamath River and Yakima lands; none reaches this order's period except as stated in the basis. The Act of June 15, 1935, sec. 3 reaches trust periods on excluded reservations not yet extended past 1936-12-31; a period that had already ended before 1934 was no longer this order's period, so its words do not reach it. IRA sec. 2 reaches only periods existing on 1934-06-18.

basis: The member's own text only amends a numbered Civil Service Rule or Schedule A or B of the 1903 rules (EO 209); its text merged into EO 209 on issue and the amending order has no command of its own after that day (ruling P2). The parent's lead (EO 209) is open.
gaps: its text continues as part of the parent until the parent ends; the parent's lifecycle carries it

only-content test: the WPA summary shows nothing but an amendment (no waiver, special rule, promulgation, prescription, construction or extension); the member's operative text uses amending words in an operative form ('is hereby amended', 'strike out', 'by adding', 'to read as follows'; title words such as 'Amending' do not count); and the text has none of the markers of a further provision (present or continued incumbents or occupants, persons now holding, serving or employed, 'it is further ordered', 'the effect of this amendment', status given to persons, a saving for incumbents). A pattern scan of all B12-B15 texts with this marker list was the measure of the test; an unmarked further provision in other words would still escape it
a compiled transcription can run into a neighbouring order

basis: Article XXI(2) of the 1947 Military Bases Agreement provides: 'Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding paragraph, the Port of Manila reservation with boundaries as of 1941 will be available for use to the United States armed forces until such time as other arrangements can be made for supply of the bases by mutual agreement of the two Governments.' The surrender in Article I of the Treaty of General Relations excepts what the United States retained by that agreement, so the surrender does not by its words reach this reservation's land, and the agreement fixes no end date. The later arrangement that ended U.S. use of the Port of Manila reservation is not held (coordinator ruling P5).
gaps: Acquire the arrangement by which the two Governments ended U.S. use of the Port of Manila reservation under art. XXI(2) (a later agreement or exchange of notes under the 1947 agreement); its date is the bound.

The 25 CFR chapter I appendix (read on the web) lists Acts of Congress continuing trust periods only for Capitan Grande, Pala, Crow, Mexican Kickapoo, Kaw, Quapaw, Klamath River and Yakima lands; none reaches this order's period except as stated in the basis. basis: The President set these reservations apart within the Canal Zone, or on adjacent lands whose use the 1903 Isthmian Canal Convention granted. The Panama Canal Treaty of 1977 entered into force on October 1, 1979, terminated and superseded the 1903 Convention (art. I(1)(a)), and returned plenary jurisdiction over the former Zone to Panama (art. XI); but U.S. military forces kept using defense sites under the Agreement in Implementation of Article IV, a new instrument that excepts that property from the transfer (coordinator ruling P5). The Treaty, and with it every U.S. right to use areas in the former Zone, terminated at noon, Panama time, December 31, 1999 (art. II: 'This Treaty shall terminate at noon, Panama time, December 31, 1999'). The Panama Canal Act of 1979 (held) treats 'Canal Zone' thereafter as the areas in the Republic of Panama made available under the Treaty (sec. 3(b)(1)) but contains no words ending these reservations earlier.

date.basis: termination of the Panama Canal Treaty of 1977 at noon on 1999-12-31 (art. II); earlier if a later order superseded or rescinded the member

gaps: The Panama Canal Treaty (1280 U.N.T.S. No. 21086) and the Agreement in Implementation of Article IV are not held; the Treaty was read on the web only. Acquire both.

A member whose land passed to Panama on October 1, 1979 (outside the defense sites) ended then; identifying those needs the Article IV agreement's annexes. Sec. 1504(a)(1) of the Panama Canal Act (held, 93 Stat. 488) authorized the Secretary of State to convey to Panama, on the Treaty's entry into force, property in the former Zone 'which is not within the land and water areas the use of which is made available to the United States'.

only-content test: the WPA summary shows nothing but an amendment (no waiver, special rule, promulgation, prescription, construction or extension); the member's operative text uses amending words in an operative form ('is hereby amended', 'strike out', 'by adding', 'to read as follows'; title words such as 'Amending' do not count); and the text has none of the markers of a further provision (present or continued incumbents or occupants, persons now holding, serving or employed, 'it is further ordered', 'the effect of this amendment', status given to persons, a saving for incumbents). basis: The order fixed a trust period that was still running on 1934-06-18 on a reservation that the held text does not place among the sec. 13 Oklahoma tribes. IRA sec. 2 by its words extended and continued "the existing periods of trust placed upon any Indian lands" until Congress directs otherwise, and this order's operative content is such a period; its stated end is therefore not a sound TERM end (P8). Whether the period, and with it the order's operative effect, was in force on 2026-10-14 depends on the reservation's IRA status and on the current state of the trust lands.
gaps: Whether the reservation came under the IRA or voted to exclude itself under sec. 18 (the election results are not held); if it excluded itself, the Act of June 15, 1935 reaches only periods not extended past 1936-12-31, and this order's own stated end may then stand.

basis: By its own terms the order performs one act: it takes the named lands out of a military or naval reservation (restoring them, relinquishing them to a territorial or Philippine government, or placing them under the Interior Department for disposal under the Act of July 5, 1884). The act was complete when the order issued; later disposal of the lands proceeds under the statute and the land laws, not under a continuing command of the order (coordinator ruling P1).
gaps: A later order could vacate a transfer to the Interior Department before disposal (EO 1011, EO 2377, EO 2563 and EO 636 did so for EO 803, EO 1422, EO 1279 and EO 372-B); a vacated transfer is ended by the vacating order (branches C09, C16, C23, C24), and the doctrine detects vacatur only where the vacating order is a member of this family. EO 3574 (Fort Davis) is decided by PLO 1712 on its own branch (P22).
Regex screens on the text decide that no reversion, retained right, redefinition or re-reservation is present; scan-OCR texts may hide such a clause.

BLM treated some Alaska transfers under the 1884 Act as continuing withdrawals: PLO 1712 (1958-08-07, held BLM table) revokes EO 3574 'entirely' and EO 7049 (four post cemeteries placed under Interior in 1935, on this branch) 'in part'. Under ruling P1 the transfer is spent on issue and the lead stands; if the owner reads such transfers as withdrawals pending disposal, Alaska members on this branch need the instrument that ended the withdrawal, and EO 7049's other tracts would be open.

Held later edges that act on the land after the order's date do not revive the spent act: EO 477 (1906) redefined the Fort Bayard reservation 'as modified by' EO 341-A; EO 5132 (1929) restored another parcel of the Hawaii Arsenal reservation that EO 3080 had also reduced; EO 4131 (1925) recites the Nulato right-of-way 'turned over to the Department of the Interior' by EO 3418. Each is flagged by the engine (acted_on_after_lead_end) and leaves the lead unchanged.

basis: The member's own text only amends a numbered Civil Service Rule or Schedule A or B of the 1903 rules (EO 209); its text merged into EO 209 on issue and the amending order has no command of its own after that day (ruling P2). The parent's lead (EO 209) is open.
gaps: its text continues as part of the parent until the parent ends; the parent's lifecycle carries it

only-content test: the WPA summary shows nothing but an amendment (no waiver, special rule, promulgation, prescription, construction or extension); the member's operative text uses amending words in an operative form ('is hereby amended', 'strike out', 'by adding', 'to read as follows'; title words such as 'Amending' do not count); and the text has none of the markers of a further provision (present or continued incumbents or occupants, persons now holding, serving or employed, 'it is further ordered', 'the effect of this amendment', status given to persons, a saving for incumbents). A pattern scan of all B12-B15 texts with this marker list was the measure of the test; an unmarked further provision in other words would still escape it
a compiled transcription can run into a neighbouring order

basis: The order only amends or adds to paragraphs of presidentially prescribed regulations (the Consular Regulations of 1896, the Instructions to Diplomatic Officers of 1897 or 1927, the Tariff of Consular Fees). Coordinator ruling P2 covers amendments of such regulations as well as of numbered orders: the order merges into the parent on issue. The parent's later history is held at least in part: EO 5642, effective July 1, 1931, cancels and replaces Article I ('The Consular Branch of the Foreign Service'), Article II ('Retirement of Foreign Service Officers'), sections 465-473 (leave of absence) and Article XXV ('Compensation of Consular Officers') of the Consular Regulations, and the parts of the Instructions to Diplomatic Officers covering the same subjects. That reaches the text inserted by at least EO 5127 (sections 465, 467), EO 5126 (Instructions VI-5) and parts of EO 3354 (Article I paragraphs) and EO 3902 and EO 1926 (paragraphs 491-492); the list is not exhaustive and changes no lead.
gaps: its text continues as part of the parent (the regulations or order amended) until the parent ends; the parent's lifecycle carries it

basis: A reservation for military, naval or departmental use stands until revoked, relinquished, transferred or disposed of. FLPMA sec. 701(c) kept every withdrawal and reservation in effect on October 21, 1976 in full force until modified, and sec. 704(a) repealed only the authority to make new ones; the Engle Act of 1958 is prospective. None of these ends or confirms a member. Many National Guard ranges were later revoked by executive orders or Public Land Orders; some reservations (for example the Fort Sill enlargement, EO 685) may still be military land. Members whose whole order a later instrument revokes by number or date are decided on branches C26-C30 and P01-P22.
gaps: A yes needs a current predicate: a statute naming the reservation, or current BLM (MLRS/LR2000) withdrawal records or DoD real property records showing the order's lands still reserved under it. A no needs the revoking order, Public Land Order, statute or surplus-property deed naming the order or its lands.

EO 2281 (Alabama military lands, 1915-12-06) carries held revocation edges from EO 5590 (1931), which revokes in part 'Executive order of December 6, 1915, creating Petroleum Reserve No. 40, Montana No. 1', a different order of the same date; the edge does not reach EO 2281. The engine flags it (persistence_lead_but_held_ending_edge); the lead stays open.

basis: By its own terms the order performs one act: it takes the named lands out of a military or naval reservation (restoring them, relinquishing them to a territorial or Philippine government, or placing them under the Interior Department for disposal under the Act of July 5, 1884). The act was complete when the order issued; later disposal of the lands proceeds under the statute and the land laws, not under a continuing command of the order (coordinator ruling P1).
gaps: A later order could vacate a transfer to the Interior Department before disposal (EO 1011, EO 2377, EO 2563 and EO 636 did so for EO 803, EO 1422, EO 1279 and EO 372-B); a vacated transfer is ended by the vacating order (branches C09, C16, C23, C24), and the doctrine detects vacatur only where the vacating order is a member of this family. EO 3574 (Fort Davis) is decided by PLO 1712 on its own branch (P22).
Regex screens on the text decide that no reversion, retained right, redefinition or re-reservation is present; scan-OCR texts may hide such a clause.

BLM treated some Alaska transfers under the 1884 Act as continuing withdrawals: PLO 1712 (1958-08-07, held BLM table) revokes EO 3574 'entirely' and EO 7049 (four post cemeteries placed under Interior in 1935, on this branch) 'in part'. Under ruling P1 the transfer is spent on issue and the lead stands; if the owner reads such transfers as withdrawals pending disposal, Alaska members on this branch need the instrument that ended the withdrawal, and EO 7049's other tracts would be open.

Held later edges that act on the land after the order's date do not revive the spent act: EO 477 (1906) redefined the Fort Bayard reservation 'as modified by' EO 341-A; EO 5132 (1929) restored another parcel of the Hawaii Arsenal reservation that EO 3080 had also reduced; EO 4131 (1925) recites the Nulato right-of-way 'turned over to the Department of the Interior' by EO 3418. Each is flagged by the engine (acted_on_after_lead_end) and leaves the lead unchanged.

basis: The member's own text only amends a numbered Civil Service Rule or Schedule A or B of the 1903 rules (EO 209); its text merged into EO 209 on issue and the amending order has no command of its own after that day (ruling P2). The parent's lead (EO 209) is open.
gaps: its text continues as part of the parent until the parent ends; the parent's lifecycle carries it

only-content test: the WPA summary shows nothing but an amendment (no waiver, special rule, promulgation, prescription, construction or extension); the member's operative text uses amending words in an operative form ('is hereby amended', 'strike out', 'by adding', 'to read as follows'; title words such as 'Amending' do not count); and the text has none of the markers of a further provision (present or continued incumbents or occupants, persons now holding, serving or employed, 'it is further ordered', 'the effect of this amendment', status given to persons, a saving for incumbents). A pattern scan of all B12-B15 texts with this marker list was the measure of the test; an unmarked further provision in other words would still escape it
a compiled transcription can run into a neighbouring order

disclosed earlier candidate end for the parent EO 209: EO 7915 and EO 8043 restated the whole text of the rules and of Schedules A and B effective 1939-02-01; under ruling P3 a restatement that does not name EO 209 does not end it, so EO 209's own lead is open

thirteen decided members carry a year-only census date (on B14: EO 508, 689, 933, 1127, 1128, 1247, 1408, 1829, 2700, 2701, 3908A and 4507; on B15: EO 3170), so their lead date is a year; several held texts give the day (EO 689: September 23, 1907; EO 933: September 3, 1908)

basis: The order authorizes (or directs) one disposition of named property under sec. 12 of the Trading with the Enemy Act and sets no deadline. It is spent when the sale, rejection, resale or release is made, and no held record shows that it was made (the one order a held text shows performed, EO 3259, is decided by B03E). The Trading with the Enemy Act is excepted from the 1921 resolution and is still law, and the later transfers of the Custodian's functions (EO 6694 of 1934; EO 9095 and EO 9142 of 1942; EO 9788 of 1946; the 1966 abolition of the Office of Alien Property) moved the functions without extinguishing authorizations, so no class event ends an unexercised authorization.
gaps: The Custodian's report for 1918 to Feb. 15, 1919 and the annual reports for 1919-1934 (S17) would show the sale or rejection for each trust; until one is held the order stays open.
Property returned under the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 254; not held) would make an unexercised authorization moot; that would need its own evidence.
Orders covering several lots or properties need one end per lot.
EO 2832 is a general rule (private sale of merchandise in lots worth no more than $10,000), not a single authorization; it ends only by revocation or supersession, which is not held.

EO 4224-A's only operative clause is 'The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to execute and deliver a quit-claim deed conveying certain interests in real estate' in Cook County, Illinois; amending EO 4073-A appears only among its stated reasons. It is its own single authorization, open here like EO 3923 and EO 4045.

EO 3183 (reject all bids at the Sept. 17, 1919 auction of the same 4,505 First Reinsurance shares): EO 3259 recites that the shares were 'thrice offered at public auction and no satisfactory bid has been received', and EO 3265 records their private sale to another buyer by Apr. 29, 1920. That shows the subject was disposed of by then, but no held text records that the Richter & Company bid was rejected; open pending a coordinator decision whether disposal of the subject ends an unexercised rejection authorization.

EO 3227 (Feb. 13, 1920) authorizes the Custodian to confirm 'in the case of sales heretofore made by him' under the Polk orders of Feb. 26, 1919 (EO 3016C) and Apr. 5, 1919 (EO 3016K). The words are conditional and name no property, so they do not show any particular sale made; EO 3016C, 3016K and 3227 stay open.

EO 3923 carries a held revocation edge from PLO 369 (May 15, 1947, 12 FR 2038; BLM table, PLO text not held): 'revoking EO Nos. 2247, 2658, and 3923; withdrawing lands for Agriculture experimental station'. EO 2247 and 2658 are Alaska agricultural-experiment-station orders; the held EO 3923 is a Custodian sale of Stoehr & Sons shares with no land to revoke. This is a number collision, so the edge does not decide this member; the PLO's '3923' should be traced in the census.
EO 4001 carries a held amendment edge from EO 4045 (1924-07-03); EO 4045 changes the parent's terms, not its performance, and both stay open.

basis: The order is an operative act on land whose forest designation persists, not a pure textual amendment, so ruling P2 does not reach it; it ends only when a later order or statute names it or expressly redescribes the forest's whole boundary while revoking prior descriptions, and no such instrument is held.
gaps: The Forest Service chronological record mapping this order to the named forest's later actions (consolidation, renaming, redescription), with the text of each later instrument to test whether it names this order or expressly redescribes the whole boundary while revoking prior descriptions.
For a persistence lead: the current Land Areas Report showing the forest or name on 2026-10-14. 16 U.S.C. 1609(a) is context only.

Where the forest the order constituted was later abolished or merged by name but the order also assigned land to another forest (for example EO 870, Holy Cross and Leadville, Holy Cross abolished by PLO 263; EO 801, Pocatello and Cache, Pocatello merged by EO 2179), ruling P7 does not reach it and the lead stays open.

basis: A reservation for military, naval or departmental use stands until revoked, relinquished, transferred or disposed of. FLPMA sec. 701(c) kept every withdrawal and reservation in effect on October 21, 1976 in full force until modified, and sec. 704(a) repealed only the authority to make new ones; the Engle Act of 1958 is prospective. None of these ends or confirms a member. Many National Guard ranges were later revoked by executive orders or Public Land Orders; some reservations (for example the Fort Sill enlargement, EO 685) may still be military land. Members whose whole order a later instrument revokes by number or date are decided on branches C26-C30 and P01-P22.
gaps: A yes needs a current predicate: a statute naming the reservation, or current BLM (MLRS/LR2000) withdrawal records or DoD real property records showing the order's lands still reserved under it. A no needs the revoking order, Public Land Order, statute or surplus-property deed naming the order or its lands.

EO 2281 (Alabama military lands, 1915-12-06) carries held revocation edges from EO 5590 (1931), which revokes in part 'Executive order of December 6, 1915, creating Petroleum Reserve No. 40, Montana No. 1', a different order of the same date; the edge does not reach EO 2281. The engine flags it (persistence_lead_but_held_ending_edge); the lead stays open.

basis: The order authorizes (or directs) one disposition of named property under sec. 12 of the Trading with the Enemy Act and sets no deadline. It is spent when the sale, rejection, resale or release is made, and no held record shows that it was made (the one order a held text shows performed, EO 3259, is decided by B03E). The Trading with the Enemy Act is excepted from the 1921 resolution and is still law, and the later transfers of the Custodian's functions (EO 6694 of 1934; EO 9095 and EO 9142 of 1942; EO 9788 of 1946; the 1966 abolition of the Office of Alien Property) moved the functions without extinguishing authorizations, so no class event ends an unexercised authorization.
gaps: The Custodian's report for 1918 to Feb. 15, 1919 and the annual reports for 1919-1934 (S17) would show the sale or rejection for each trust; until one is held the order stays open.
Property returned under the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 254; not held) would make an unexercised authorization moot; that would need its own evidence.
Orders covering several lots or properties need one end per lot.
EO 2832 is a general rule (private sale of merchandise in lots worth no more than $10,000), not a single authorization; it ends only by revocation or supersession, which is not held.

EO 4224-A's only operative clause is 'The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to execute and deliver a quit-claim deed conveying certain interests in real estate' in Cook County, Illinois; amending EO 4073-A appears only among its stated reasons. It is its own single authorization, open here like EO 3923 and EO 4045.

EO 3183 (reject all bids at the Sept. 17, 1919 auction of the same 4,505 First Reinsurance shares): EO 3259 recites that the shares were 'thrice offered at public auction and no satisfactory bid has been received', and EO 3265 records their private sale to another buyer by Apr. 29, 1920. That shows the subject was disposed of by then, but no held text records that the Richter & Company bid was rejected; open pending a coordinator decision whether disposal of the subject ends an unexercised rejection authorization.

EO 3227 (Feb. 13, 1920) authorizes the Custodian to confirm 'in the case of sales heretofore made by him' under the Polk orders of Feb. 26, 1919 (EO 3016C) and Apr. 5, 1919 (EO 3016K). The words are conditional and name no property, so they do not show any particular sale made; EO 3016C, 3016K and 3227 stay open.

EO 3923 carries a held revocation edge from PLO 369 (May 15, 1947, 12 FR 2038; BLM table, PLO text not held): 'revoking EO Nos. 2247, 2658, and 3923; withdrawing lands for Agriculture experimental station'. EO 2247 and 2658 are Alaska agricultural-experiment-station orders; the held EO 3923 is a Custodian sale of Stoehr & Sons shares with no land to revoke. This is a number collision, so the edge does not decide this member; the PLO's '3923' should be traced in the census.
EO 4001 carries a held amendment edge from EO 4045 (1924-07-03); EO 4045 changes the parent's terms, not its performance, and both stay open.

basis: By its own terms the order performs one act: it takes the named lands out of a military or naval reservation (restoring them, relinquishing them to a territorial or Philippine government, or placing them under the Interior Department for disposal under the Act of July 5, 1884). The act was complete when the order issued; later disposal of the lands proceeds under the statute and the land laws, not under a continuing command of the order (coordinator ruling P1).
gaps: A later order could vacate a transfer to the Interior Department before disposal (EO 1011, EO 2377, EO 2563 and EO 636 did so for EO 803, EO 1422, EO 1279 and EO 372-B); a vacated transfer is ended by the vacating order (branches C09, C16, C23, C24), and the doctrine detects vacatur only where the vacating order is a member of this family. EO 3574 (Fort Davis) is decided by PLO 1712 on its own branch (P22).
Regex screens on the text decide that no reversion, retained right, redefinition or re-reservation is present; scan-OCR texts may hide such a clause.

BLM treated some Alaska transfers under the 1884 Act as continuing withdrawals: PLO 1712 (1958-08-07, held BLM table) revokes EO 3574 'entirely' and EO 7049 (four post cemeteries placed under Interior in 1935, on this branch) 'in part'. Under ruling P1 the transfer is spent on issue and the lead stands; if the owner reads such transfers as withdrawals pending disposal, Alaska members on this branch need the instrument that ended the withdrawal, and EO 7049's other tracts would be open.

Held later edges that act on the land after the order's date do not revive the spent act: EO 477 (1906) redefined the Fort Bayard reservation 'as modified by' EO 341-A; EO 5132 (1929) restored another parcel of the Hawaii Arsenal reservation that EO 3080 had also reduced; EO 4131 (1925) recites the Nulato right-of-way 'turned over to the Department of the Interior' by EO 3418. Each is flagged by the engine (acted_on_after_lead_end) and leaves the lead unchanged.

basis: A lighthouse reservation continues until revoked by order or PLO, or until the station is conveyed; the 1939 transfer of the Bureau of Lighthouses to the Coast Guard and transfers of jurisdiction (for example EO 6896 moving San Miguel and Prince Islands to the Navy) continue it. gaps: Two held later edges are flagged by the engine as ending edges on this persistence-kind open lead; neither is a full end: PLO 1724 (1958) revokes EO 431 ("EOs of ... Mar. 27, 1906") only "in part" per the BLM table; PLO 7391 (1999) revokes an Oregon power-site order of November 14, 1917 (Power Site Reserve No. 658), a date collision with EO 2755, not EO 2755 itself.

Search the BLM PLO tables (held) and Federal Register for a PLO naming the order by number or date; the 1867-1906 and Alaska multi-site orders (for example EO 4257, revoked in part by six PLOs 1960-1994) need site-by-site review.

Later held BLM headings show partial revocations only: PLO 7583 (2003) of the Ediz Hook Lighthouse Reservation (reduced by EO 2646), and PLO 7723 (2008) of lighthouse withdrawals for Channel Islands National Park, which may reach the San Miguel, Prince and Santa Barbara Island orders (EO 1066, 2750, 347B, 6896); which lands they released is not identified in a held copy.
Light stations conveyed under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act (2000) or surplus-property law end by deed; GSA and NPS conveyance lists are not held.

basis: Article XXI(2) of the 1947 Military Bases Agreement provides: 'Notwithstanding the provisions of the preceding paragraph, the Port of Manila reservation with boundaries as of 1941 will be available for use to the United States armed forces until such time as other arrangements can be made for supply of the bases by mutual agreement of the two Governments.' The surrender in Article I of the Treaty of General Relations excepts what the United States retained by that agreement, so the surrender does not by its words reach this reservation's land, and the agreement fixes no end date. The later arrangement that ended U.S. use of the Port of Manila reservation is not held (coordinator ruling P5).
gaps: Acquire the arrangement by which the two Governments ended U.S. use of the Port of Manila reservation under art. XXI(2) (a later agreement or exchange of notes under the 1947 agreement); its date is the bound.

Whether each member's tract lay inside 'the Port of Manila reservation with boundaries as of 1941' needs the 1941 boundary; EO 4787 also reserves part of the former Regan Barracks reservation in Albay, which is outside Manila; EO 1298 also modifies other Manila reservations (several of which it returned to the Philippine Government).

basis: By its own terms the order performs one act: it takes the named lands out of a military or naval reservation (restoring them, relinquishing them to a territorial or Philippine government, or placing them under the Interior Department for disposal under the Act of July 5, 1884). The act was complete when the order issued; later disposal of the lands proceeds under the statute and the land laws, not under a continuing command of the order (coordinator ruling P1).
gaps: A later order could vacate a transfer to the Interior Department before disposal (EO 1011, EO 2377, EO 2563 and EO 636 did so for EO 803, EO 1422, EO 1279 and EO 372-B); a vacated transfer is ended by the vacating order (branches C09, C16, C23, C24), and the doctrine detects vacatur only where the vacating order is a member of this family. EO 3574 (Fort Davis) is decided by PLO 1712 on its own branch (P22).
Regex screens on the text decide that no reversion, retained right, redefinition or re-reservation is present; scan-OCR texts may hide such a clause.

BLM treated some Alaska transfers under the 1884 Act as continuing withdrawals: PLO 1712 (1958-08-07, held BLM table) revokes EO 3574 'entirely' and EO 7049 (four post cemeteries placed under Interior in 1935, on this branch) 'in part'. Under ruling P1 the transfer is spent on issue and the lead stands; if the owner reads such transfers as withdrawals pending disposal, Alaska members on this branch need the instrument that ended the withdrawal, and EO 7049's other tracts would be open.

Held later edges that act on the land after the order's date do not revive the spent act: EO 477 (1906) redefined the Fort Bayard reservation 'as modified by' EO 341-A; EO 5132 (1929) restored another parcel of the Hawaii Arsenal reservation that EO 3080 had also reduced; EO 4131 (1925) recites the Nulato right-of-way 'turned over to the Department of the Interior' by EO 3418. Each is flagged by the engine (acted_on_after_lead_end) and leaves the lead unchanged.

only-content test: the WPA summary shows nothing but an amendment (no waiver, special rule, promulgation, prescription, construction or extension); the member's operative text uses amending words in an operative form ('is hereby amended', 'strike out', 'by adding', 'to read as follows'; title words such as 'Amending' do not count); and the text has none of the markers of a further provision (present or continued incumbents or occupants, persons now holding, serving or employed, 'it is further ordered', 'the effect of this amendment', status given to persons, a saving for incumbents). A pattern scan of all B12-B15 texts with this marker list was the measure of the test; an unmarked further provision in other words would still escape it

The surrender in Article I of the Treaty of General Relations excepts what the United States retained by that agreement, so the surrender does not by its words reach this reservation's land, and the agreement fixes no end date. The later arrangement that ended U.S. use of the Port of Manila reservation is not held (coordinator ruling P5).
gaps: Acquire the arrangement by which the two Governments ended U.S. use of the Port of Manila reservation under art. XXI(2) (a later agreement or exchange of notes under the 1947 agreement); its date is the bound.

Whether each member's tract lay inside 'the Port of Manila reservation with boundaries as of 1941' needs the 1941 boundary; EO 4787 also reserves part of the former Regan Barracks reservation in Albay, which is outside Manila; EO 1298 also modifies other Manila reservations (several of which it returned to the Philippine Government).

basis: By its own terms the order performs one act: it takes the named lands out of a military or naval reservation (restoring them, relinquishing them to a territorial or Philippine government, or placing them under the Interior Department for disposal under the Act of July 5, 1884). The act was complete when the order issued; later disposal of the lands proceeds under the statute and the land laws, not under a continuing command of the order (coordinator ruling P1).
gaps: A later order could vacate a transfer to the Interior Department before disposal (EO 1011, EO 2377, EO 2563 and EO 636 did so for EO 803, EO 1422, EO 1279 and EO 372-B); a vacated transfer is ended by the vacating order (branches C09, C16, C23, C24), and the doctrine detects vacatur only where the vacating order is a member of this family. EO 3574 (Fort Davis) is decided by PLO 1712 on its own branch (P22).
Regex screens on the text decide that no reversion, retained right, redefinition or re-reservation is present; scan-OCR texts may hide such a clause.

BLM treated some Alaska transfers under the 1884 Act as continuing withdrawals: PLO 1712 (1958-08-07, held BLM table) revokes EO 3574 'entirely' and EO 7049 (four post cemeteries placed under Interior in 1935, on this branch) 'in part'. Under ruling P1 the transfer is spent on issue and the lead stands; if the owner reads such transfers as withdrawals pending disposal, Alaska members on this branch need the instrument that ended the withdrawal, and EO 7049's other tracts would be open.

Held later edges that act on the land after the order's date do not revive the spent act: EO 477 (1906) redefined the Fort Bayard reservation 'as modified by' EO 341-A; EO 5132 (1929) restored another parcel of the Hawaii Arsenal reservation that EO 3080 had also reduced; EO 4131 (1925) recites the Nulato right-of-way 'turned over to the Department of the Interior' by EO 3418. Each is flagged by the engine (acted_on_after_lead_end) and leaves the lead unchanged.

Light stations conveyed under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act (2000) or surplus-property law end by deed; GSA and NPS conveyance lists are not held.

basis: The member's own text only amends a numbered Civil Service Rule or Schedule A or B of the 1903 rules (EO 209); its text merged into EO 209 on issue and the amending order has no command of its own after that day (ruling P2). The parent's lead (EO 209) is open.
gaps: its text continues as part of the parent until the parent ends; the parent's lifecycle carries it

only-content test: the WPA summary shows nothing but an amendment (no waiver, special rule, promulgation, prescription, construction or extension); the member's operative text uses amending words in an operative form ('is hereby amended', 'strike out', 'by adding', 'to read as follows'; title words such as 'Amending' do not count); and the text has none of the markers of a further provision (present or continued incumbents or occupants, persons now holding, serving or employed, 'it is further ordered', 'the effect of this amendment', status given to persons, a saving for incumbents). A pattern scan of all B12-B15 texts with this marker list was the measure of the test; an unmarked further provision in other words would still escape it
a compiled transcription can run into a neighbouring order

disclosed earlier candidate end for the parent EO 209: EO 7915 and EO 8043 restated the whole text of the rules and of Schedules A and B effective 1939-02-01; under ruling P3 a restatement that does not name EO 209 does not end it, so EO 209's own lead is open

basis: The order only amends or adds to paragraphs of presidentially prescribed regulations (the Consular Regulations of 1896, the Instructions to Diplomatic Officers of 1897 or 1927, the Tariff of Consular Fees). Coordinator ruling P2 covers amendments of such regulations as well as of numbered orders: the order merges into the parent on issue. The parent's later history is held at least in part: EO 5642, effective July 1, 1931, cancels and replaces Article I ('The Consular Branch of the Foreign Service'), Article II ('Retirement of Foreign Service Officers'), sections 465-473 (leave of absence) and Article XXV ('Compensation of Consular Officers') of the Consular Regulations, and the parts of the Instructions to Diplomatic Officers covering the same subjects. That reaches the text inserted by at least EO 5127 (sections 465, 467), EO 5126 (Instructions VI-5) and parts of EO 3354 (Article I paragraphs) and EO 3902 and EO 1926 (paragraphs 491-492); the list is not exhaustive and changes no lead.
gaps: its text continues as part of the parent (the regulations or order amended) until the parent ends; the parent's lifecycle carries it

Under P2 that is a later event of the parent regulations, not a command of EO 610.

basis: A reservation for military, naval or departmental use stands until revoked, relinquished, transferred or disposed of. FLPMA sec. 701(c) kept every withdrawal and reservation in effect on October 21, 1976 in full force until modified, and sec. 704(a) repealed only the authority to make new ones; the Engle Act of 1958 is prospective. None of these ends or confirms a member. Many National Guard ranges were later revoked by executive orders or Public Land Orders; some reservations (for example the Fort Sill enlargement, EO 685) may still be military land. Members whose whole order a later instrument revokes by number or date are decided on branches C26-C30 and P01-P22.
gaps: A yes needs a current predicate: a statute naming the reservation, or current BLM (MLRS/LR2000) withdrawal records or DoD real property records showing the order's lands still reserved under it. A no needs the revoking order, Public Land Order, statute or surplus-property deed naming the order or its lands.

basis: The order authorizes (or directs) one disposition of named property under sec. 12 of the Trading with the Enemy Act and sets no deadline. It is spent when the sale, rejection, resale or release is made, and no held record shows that it was made (the one order a held text shows performed, EO 3259, is decided by B03E). The Trading with the Enemy Act is excepted from the 1921 resolution and is still law, and the later transfers of the Custodian's functions (EO 6694 of 1934; EO 9095 and EO 9142 of 1942; EO 9788 of 1946; the 1966 abolition of the Office of Alien Property) moved the functions without extinguishing authorizations, so no class event ends an unexercised authorization.
gaps: The Custodian's report for 1918 to Feb. 15, 1919 and the annual reports for 1919-1934 (S17) would show the sale or rejection for each trust; until one is held the order stays open.
Property returned under the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 254; not held) would make an unexercised authorization moot; that would need its own evidence.
Orders covering several lots or properties need one end per lot.
EO 2832 is a general rule (private sale of merchandise in lots worth no more than $10,000), not a single authorization; it ends only by revocation or supersession, which is not held.

EO 4224-A's only operative clause is 'The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to execute and deliver a quit-claim deed conveying certain interests in real estate' in Cook County, Illinois; amending EO 4073-A appears only among its stated reasons. It is its own single authorization, open here like EO 3923 and EO 4045.

EO 3183 (reject all bids at the Sept. 17, 1919 auction of the same 4,505 First Reinsurance shares): EO 3259 recites that the shares were 'thrice offered at public auction and no satisfactory bid has been received', and EO 3265 records their private sale to another buyer by Apr. 29, 1920. That shows the subject was disposed of by then, but no held text records that the Richter & Company bid was rejected; open pending a coordinator decision whether disposal of the subject ends an unexercised rejection authorization.

EO 3227 (Feb. 13, 1920) authorizes the Custodian to confirm 'in the case of sales heretofore made by him' under the Polk orders of Feb. 26, 1919 (EO 3016C) and Apr. 5, 1919 (EO 3016K). The words are conditional and name no property, so they do not show any particular sale made; EO 3016C, 3016K and 3227 stay open.

EO 3923 carries a held revocation edge from PLO 369 (May 15, 1947, 12 FR 2038; BLM table, PLO text not held): 'revoking EO Nos. 2247, 2658, and 3923; withdrawing lands for Agriculture experimental station'. EO 2247 and 2658 are Alaska agricultural-experiment-station orders; the held EO 3923 is a Custodian sale of Stoehr & Sons shares with no land to revoke. This is a number collision, so the edge does not decide this member; the PLO's '3923' should be traced in the census.
EO 4001 carries a held amendment edge from EO 4045 (1924-07-03); EO 4045 changes the parent's terms, not its performance, and both stay open.

basis: The order authorizes (or directs) one disposition of named property under sec. 12 of the Trading with the Enemy Act and sets no deadline. It is spent when the sale, rejection, resale or release is made, and no held record shows that it was made (the one order a held text shows performed, EO 3259, is decided by B03E). The Trading with the Enemy Act is excepted from the 1921 resolution and is still law, and the later transfers of the Custodian's functions (EO 6694 of 1934; EO 9095 and EO 9142 of 1942; EO 9788 of 1946; the 1966 abolition of the Office of Alien Property) moved the functions without extinguishing authorizations, so no class event ends an unexercised authorization.
gaps: The Custodian's report for 1918 to Feb. 15, 1919 and the annual reports for 1919-1934 (S17) would show the sale or rejection for each trust; until one is held the order stays open.
Property returned under the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 254; not held) would make an unexercised authorization moot; that would need its own evidence.
Orders covering several lots or properties need one end per lot.
EO 2832 is a general rule (private sale of merchandise in lots worth no more than $10,000), not a single authorization; it ends only by revocation or supersession, which is not held.

EO 4224-A's only operative clause is 'The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to execute and deliver a quit-claim deed conveying certain interests in real estate' in Cook County, Illinois; amending EO 4073-A appears only among its stated reasons. It is its own single authorization, open here like EO 3923 and EO 4045.

EO 3183 (reject all bids at the Sept. 17, 1919 auction of the same 4,505 First Reinsurance shares): EO 3259 recites that the shares were 'thrice offered at public auction and no satisfactory bid has been received', and EO 3265 records their private sale to another buyer by Apr. 29, 1920. That shows the subject was disposed of by then, but no held text records that the Richter & Company bid was rejected; open pending a coordinator decision whether disposal of the subject ends an unexercised rejection authorization.

EO 3227 (Feb. 13, 1920) authorizes the Custodian to confirm 'in the case of sales heretofore made by him' under the Polk orders of Feb. 26, 1919 (EO 3016C) and Apr. 5, 1919 (EO 3016K). The words are conditional and name no property, so they do not show any particular sale made; EO 3016C, 3016K and 3227 stay open.

EO 3923 carries a held revocation edge from PLO 369 (May 15, 1947, 12 FR 2038; BLM table, PLO text not held): 'revoking EO Nos. 2247, 2658, and 3923; withdrawing lands for Agriculture experimental station'. EO 2247 and 2658 are Alaska agricultural-experiment-station orders; the held EO 3923 is a Custodian sale of Stoehr & Sons shares with no land to revoke. This is a number collision, so the edge does not decide this member; the PLO's '3923' should be traced in the census.
EO 4001 carries a held amendment edge from EO 4045 (1924-07-03); EO 4045 changes the parent's terms, not its performance, and both stay open.

basis: By its own terms the order performs one act: it takes the named lands out of a military or naval reservation (restoring them, relinquishing them to a territorial or Philippine government, or placing them under the Interior Department for disposal under the Act of July 5, 1884). The act was complete when the order issued; later disposal of the lands proceeds under the statute and the land laws, not under a continuing command of the order (coordinator ruling P1).
gaps: A later order could vacate a transfer to the Interior Department before disposal (EO 1011, EO 2377, EO 2563 and EO 636 did so for EO 803, EO 1422, EO 1279 and EO 372-B); a vacated transfer is ended by the vacating order (branches C09, C16, C23, C24), and the doctrine detects vacatur only where the vacating order is a member of this family. EO 3574 (Fort Davis) is decided by PLO 1712 on its own branch (P22).
Regex screens on the text decide that no reversion, retained right, redefinition or re-reservation is present; scan-OCR texts may hide such a clause.

BLM treated some Alaska transfers under the 1884 Act as continuing withdrawals: PLO 1712 (1958-08-07, held BLM table) revokes EO 3574 'entirely' and EO 7049 (four post cemeteries placed under Interior in 1935, on this branch) 'in part'. Under ruling P1 the transfer is spent on issue and the lead stands; if the owner reads such transfers as withdrawals pending disposal, Alaska members on this branch need the instrument that ended the withdrawal, and EO 7049's other tracts would be open.

Held later edges that act on the land after the order's date do not revive the spent act: EO 477 (1906) redefined the Fort Bayard reservation 'as modified by' EO 341-A; EO 5132 (1929) restored another parcel of the Hawaii Arsenal reservation that EO 3080 had also reduced; EO 4131 (1925) recites the Nulato right-of-way 'turned over to the Department of the Interior' by EO 3418. Each is flagged by the engine (acted_on_after_lead_end) and leaves the lead unchanged.

basis: The order extends the trust period on the lands it covers for a stated number of years, and the whole extended period ran out before 1934-06-18; by its own terms its operation ended then. IRA sec. 2 reaches only trust periods existing on 1934-06-18, so it did not reach this period; any later continuation of the trust on the same land came from a separate later executive order with its own lifecycle, or from a statute named in the gaps.

date.basis: stated expiry plus stated period (see doctrine appendix)

gaps: Later held extension orders naming the same tribe, band or class (each a separate executive order with its own lifecycle; it may cover other allotments): 3445: EO 5575; 3446: EO 5580; 3447: EO 5415, EO 5626; 3586: EO 5734.
Expiry year and period are read from the order text (the WPA 1944 summary where the scan is illegible); individual allotment expiry dates are not held, so the end is an interval.

The 25 CFR chapter I appendix (read on the web) lists Acts of Congress continuing trust periods only for Capitan Grande, Pala, Crow, Mexican Kickapoo, Kaw, Quapaw, Klamath River and Yakima lands; none reaches this order's period except as stated in the basis. The Act of June 15, 1935, sec. 3 reaches trust periods on excluded reservations not yet extended past 1936-12-31; a period that had already ended before 1934 was no longer this order's period, so its words do not reach it. IRA sec. 2 reaches only periods existing on 1934-06-18.

basis: The order authorizes (or directs) one disposition of named property under sec. 12 of the Trading with the Enemy Act and sets no deadline. It is spent when the sale, rejection, resale or release is made, and no held record shows that it was made (the one order a held text shows performed, EO 3259, is decided by B03E). The Trading with the Enemy Act is excepted from the 1921 resolution and is still law, and the later transfers of the Custodian's functions (EO 6694 of 1934; EO 9095 and EO 9142 of 1942; EO 9788 of 1946; the 1966 abolition of the Office of Alien Property) moved the functions without extinguishing authorizations, so no class event ends an unexercised authorization.
gaps: The Custodian's report for 1918 to Feb. 15, 1919 and the annual reports for 1919-1934 (S17) would show the sale or rejection for each trust; until one is held the order stays open.
Property returned under the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 254; not held) would make an unexercised authorization moot; that would need its own evidence.
Orders covering several lots or properties need one end per lot.
EO 2832 is a general rule (private sale of merchandise in lots worth no more than $10,000), not a single authorization; it ends only by revocation or supersession, which is not held.

EO 4224-A's only operative clause is 'The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to execute and deliver a quit-claim deed conveying certain interests in real estate' in Cook County, Illinois; amending EO 4073-A appears only among its stated reasons. It is its own single authorization, open here like EO 3923 and EO 4045.

EO 3183 (reject all bids at the Sept. 17, 1919 auction of the same 4,505 First Reinsurance shares): EO 3259 recites that the shares were 'thrice offered at public auction and no satisfactory bid has been received', and EO 3265 records their private sale to another buyer by Apr. 29, 1920. basis: The order authorizes (or directs) one disposition of named property under sec. 12 of the Trading with the Enemy Act and sets no deadline. It is spent when the sale, rejection, resale or release is made, and no held record shows that it was made (the one order a held text shows performed, EO 3259, is decided by B03E). The Trading with the Enemy Act is excepted from the 1921 resolution and is still law, and the later transfers of the Custodian's functions (EO 6694 of 1934; EO 9095 and EO 9142 of 1942; EO 9788 of 1946; the 1966 abolition of the Office of Alien Property) moved the functions without extinguishing authorizations, so no class event ends an unexercised authorization.
gaps: The Custodian's report for 1918 to Feb. 15, 1919 and the annual reports for 1919-1934 (S17) would show the sale or rejection for each trust; until one is held the order stays open.
Property returned under the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 254; not held) would make an unexercised authorization moot; that would need its own evidence.
Orders covering several lots or properties need one end per lot.
EO 2832 is a general rule (private sale of merchandise in lots worth no more than $10,000), not a single authorization; it ends only by revocation or supersession, which is not held.

EO 4224-A's only operative clause is 'The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to execute and deliver a quit-claim deed conveying certain interests in real estate' in Cook County, Illinois; amending EO 4073-A appears only among its stated reasons. It is its own single authorization, open here like EO 3923 and EO 4045.

EO 3183 (reject all bids at the Sept. 17, 1919 auction of the same 4,505 First Reinsurance shares): EO 3259 recites that the shares were 'thrice offered at public auction and no satisfactory bid has been received', and EO 3265 records their private sale to another buyer by Apr. 29, 1920. That shows the subject was disposed of by then, but no held text records that the Richter & Company bid was rejected; open pending a coordinator decision whether disposal of the subject ends an unexercised rejection authorization.

EO 3227 (Feb. 13, 1920) authorizes the Custodian to confirm 'in the case of sales heretofore made by him' under the Polk orders of Feb. 26, 1919 (EO 3016C) and Apr. 5, 1919 (EO 3016K). The words are conditional and name no property, so they do not show any particular sale made; EO 3016C, 3016K and 3227 stay open.

EO 3923 carries a held revocation edge from PLO 369 (May 15, 1947, 12 FR 2038; BLM table, PLO text not held): 'revoking EO Nos. 2247, 2658, and 3923; withdrawing lands for Agriculture experimental station'. EO 2247 and 2658 are Alaska agricultural-experiment-station orders; the held EO 3923 is a Custodian sale of Stoehr & Sons shares with no land to revoke. This is a number collision, so the edge does not decide this member; the PLO's '3923' should be traced in the census.
EO 4001 carries a held amendment edge from EO 4045 (1924-07-03); EO 4045 changes the parent's terms, not its performance, and both stay open.
